What a /8 means

A /8 is a very large block, the size of a historic Class A. 10.0.0.0/8 is the best-known private example.

The prefix length is the number of leading bits that identify the network. A /8 uses 8 network bits and leaves 24 host bits, so the block contains 16,777,216 addresses. Usable hosts: 2(32−8) − 2 = 16,777,216 − 2 = 16,777,214.

Configuration examples

Cisco IOS

interface Vlan10
 ip address 10.0.0.1 255.0.0.0
!
access-list 10 permit 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255

Juniper Junos

set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family inet address 10.0.0.1/8

Linux

ip addr add 10.0.0.1/8 dev eth0

Addresses shown are examples from private or documentation space. Replace them with your own plan.

FAQ

How many usable hosts are in a /8?

16,777,214. A /8 has 16,777,216 addresses; the first is the network address and the last is the broadcast address, so 16,777,214 are usable.

What is the subnet mask for /8?

255.0.0.0. The wildcard mask, used in ACLs and OSPF network statements, is 0.255.255.255.
